title: Tim Curry, ‘Rocky Horror Picture Show’ Star, Dies at 80
summary: Tim Curry, who soared to fame in the ‘70s as the flamboyant star of the campy horror movie stage spoof “The Rocky Horror Show” and its screen version “The Rocky Horror Picture Show,” died on Tuesday in Los Angeles, Variety has confirmed. He was 80. A cause of death was not…
whatHappening: Tim Curry, the iconic actor and singer best known for his role as Dr. Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Picture Show, has died at age 80 in Los Angeles. The British performer, who became a cultural phenomenon through the campy 1975 film and its stage predecessor, passed away on Tuesday.
whoInvolved: Tim Curry was a British actor and singer who rose to prominence in the 1970s for his villainous and flamboyant roles on stage and screen. He earned an Emmy Award and received nominations for Grammy, Olivier, and Tony Awards throughout his career, becoming most famous for originating the role of Dr. Frank-N-Furter in both the 1973 stage musical and 1975 film adaptation of The Rocky Horror Show.
whyMatters: Curry's death marks the end of an era for one of theater and film's most distinctive performers, whose portrayal of Dr. Frank-N-Furter became an enduring touchstone in popular culture. The Rocky Horror Picture Show evolved into a cult classic with decades of midnight screenings and audience participation, cementing Curry's legacy as an influential figure who helped define a generation's approach to camp and gender-bending performance art.
articleBody:
Tim Curry, the flamboyant British actor and singer who became a cultural icon through his portrayal of Dr. Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Picture Show, has died at 80 in Los Angeles, Variety reports. The cause of death was not immediately disclosed. Curry's death represents the loss of one of entertainment's most distinctive and versatile performers, whose career spanned decades of theatrical and film work.

Curry first achieved fame in the early 1970s when he originated the role of Dr. Frank-N-Furter in the stage musical The Rocky Horror Show, which premiered in 1973 and ran through 1975. His performance was nothing short of transformative—a flamboyant, sexually provocative portrayal that pushed theatrical boundaries and made him an overnight sensation. Two years after the stage show debuted, director Jim Sharman adapted the musical into a film, with Curry reprising his signature role in The Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975), which was produced by Lou Adler and Michael White and distributed by 20th Century Fox.

The Rocky Horror Picture Show, based on Richard O'Brien's original music, book, and lyrics, became far more than a mere film adaptation. It evolved into a genuine cultural phenomenon, spawning decades of midnight screenings in theaters across the country where audiences dressed in costume and participated in audience-participation traditions that became as legendary as the film itself. Curry's performance at the center of this spectacle—his commanding stage presence, his vocal ability, and his fearless commitment to a gender-nonconforming character—was the engine that made the entire enterprise work.

Beyond The Rocky Horror Picture Show, Curry built a formidable career as a performer known for his villainous and theatrical roles. He earned an Emmy Award and received nominations for a Grammy Award, two Olivier Awards, and three Tony Awards, reflecting the breadth of his work across theater, film, and television. His ability to inhabit complex, often unsettling characters made him a sought-after talent for decades, though it was always his early triumph as Dr. Frank-N-Furter that remained most visible to the general public.

Curry's legacy extends beyond his individual performances to his influence on how performers approach camp, theatrical expression, and the portrayal of characters who defy conventional categories. His work helped establish The Rocky Horror Picture Show as an enduring artifact of popular culture, one that continues to attract new generations of viewers and participants. The film's lasting appeal owes much to Curry's uncompromising performance and the cultural space he helped create for alternative and transgressive art.

title: Iowa and Montana Ask Supreme Court to Block ‘Politicized’ Paramount-Warner Bros. Antitrust Suit Filed by California and 11 Other States
summary: Two Republican attorneys general are hoping the Supreme Court will step in to stop the antitrust lawsuit filed by 12 Democratic state AGs seeking to block Paramount’s takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery. Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird and Montana AG Austin Knudsen filed a…
whatHappening: Iowa and Montana's Republican attorneys general have asked the Supreme Court to block an antitrust lawsuit filed by 12 Democratic state attorneys general seeking to prevent Paramount's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The Republican officials are characterizing the suit as politically motivated rather than based on legitimate competitive concerns.
whoInvolved: Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird and Montana Attorney General Austin Knudsen represent the Republican-led challenge. On the opposing side are 12 Democratic state attorneys general pursuing the antitrust case against Paramount Global, a major entertainment conglomerate formed in 2019 through the merger of Viacom and CBS Corporation, and Warner Bros. Discovery, created in 2022 from the merger of WarnerMedia and Discovery, Inc.
whyMatters: The dispute reveals a deep partisan divide over whether major media consolidation poses genuine antitrust concerns or reflects political grandstanding. The outcome could affect not only this specific deal but set precedent for how states coordinate on antitrust enforcement and whether Supreme Court intervention in state-level litigation becomes routine in high-profile corporate transactions.
articleBody:
Two Republican state attorneys general are escalating their challenge to a multistate antitrust lawsuit by asking the Supreme Court to intervene and block the case entirely. Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird and Montana Attorney General Austin Knudsen filed the emergency petition, arguing that the suit filed by 12 Democratic-led states against Paramount's proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery is driven by partisan politics rather than legitimate antitrust principles.

The antitrust action itself targets one of the entertainment industry's most significant consolidation attempts in recent years. Paramount Global, formed on December 4, 2019, through the merger of Viacom and CBS Corporation, is seeking to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery, the sprawling media conglomerate created through the 2022 merger of WarnerMedia and Discovery, Inc. The deal would combine two of the largest players in streaming, traditional television, and film production.

According to Variety, the Republican attorneys general contend that the Democratic states' lawsuit represents a coordinated political effort rather than sound antitrust enforcement. Their petition to the Supreme Court seeks to have the lower court proceedings halted pending review, though the exact legal mechanism for the challenge remains unclear from available reporting. The move reflects growing tensions between state and federal regulatory approaches to media consolidation, particularly given that federal regulators have their own review processes for such major transactions.

The partisan split on the deal is unusual in antitrust enforcement, which has historically transcended party lines when addressing concerns about market concentration. Democratic states argue that the merger would reduce competition in streaming, cable, and broadcast television, while the Republican attorneys general appear to view the lawsuit as an attempt to use antitrust law for political purposes. This framing suggests a broader dispute about the proper role of antitrust doctrine in high-profile corporate transactions.

The Supreme Court petition adds another layer of complexity to what is already a multifaceted regulatory review process. Beyond state-level litigation, the transaction faces scrutiny from federal antitrust enforcers and industry analysts. The competing legal challenges underscore how consolidation in media—an industry with significant influence over public discourse—has become a flashpoint for ideological and partisan disagreement about how markets should be regulated and by whom.

title: Korea’s DRX Signs Strategic Partnership With Indonesia’s Nuon to Expand Gaming and Entertainment Ties (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Korea’s DRX Corp. and PT Nuon Digital Indonesia signed a strategic partnership in Jakarta to expand gaming and entertainment ties between Indonesia and Korea, starting with an entertainment festival called DRX Homefront Indonesia and a joint game publishing initiative between…
whatHappening: South Korea's DRX Corp. and Indonesian firm PT Nuon Digital Indonesia have formalized a strategic partnership designed to deepen gaming and entertainment collaboration between the two countries. The deal will launch with an entertainment festival called DRX Homefront Indonesia and a joint game publishing venture.
whoInvolved: DRX Corp. is a South Korean gaming and entertainment company, while PT Nuon Digital Indonesia is a digital entertainment firm based in Indonesia. The partnership was signed in Jakarta and represents a cross-border effort to tap into growing gaming markets in Southeast Asia.
whyMatters: The partnership signals expanding Korean entertainment and gaming influence in Southeast Asia's largest economy and most populous country. It positions both companies to capitalize on Indonesia's rapidly growing digital gaming audience while establishing distribution and content creation infrastructure that could serve as a model for broader regional expansion.
articleBody:
Korea's DRX Corp. and PT Nuon Digital Indonesia have signed a strategic partnership in Jakarta aimed at expanding gaming and entertainment ties between South Korea and Indonesia, according to Variety. The collaboration marks a significant step in Korean entertainment companies' efforts to establish deeper roots in Southeast Asia's largest market. The partnership will launch with two major initiatives: an entertainment festival branded as DRX Homefront Indonesia and a joint game publishing operation that will bring titles to Indonesian audiences.

The entertainment festival represents a direct effort to build brand awareness and community engagement in Indonesia. By creating a localized event under the DRX brand, both companies aim to tap into Indonesia's substantial gaming and esports enthusiast base. The joint publishing initiative will handle the distribution and localization of games, allowing both partners to leverage their respective strengths—DRX's experience in content creation and gaming properties alongside Nuon's established presence and relationships within the Indonesian market.

Indonesia has emerged as one of Southeast Asia's fastest-growing gaming markets, driven by rising internet penetration, smartphone adoption, and a young demographic with disposable income. The country's gaming population has expanded significantly over the past decade, creating opportunities for both domestic and international players to establish footholds. By establishing this partnership now, DRX and Nuon position themselves to capture a portion of this expanding audience as esports and gaming entertainment continue to mature in the region.

The strategic nature of the partnership suggests both companies are thinking beyond immediate commercial returns. By creating localized content and festivals, they're building the kind of grassroots engagement that can sustain long-term market presence. Korean entertainment companies have found particular success in Southeast Asian markets, leveraging cultural affinity and expertise in digital content production. This partnership follows a broader pattern of Korean firms seeking to establish operations and distribution networks across the region.

The DRX Homefront Indonesia festival and publishing initiative represent concrete steps toward making both companies meaningful players in Indonesia's entertainment ecosystem rather than distant foreign entities. Success in Indonesia could serve as a template for expansion into other Southeast Asian nations, making this partnership a potential turning point for DRX's regional strategy.

title: Netflix’ Latest Marketing Mash-Up Pairs Stella Artois With ‘The Gentlemen’
summary: Netflix has what looks to be a great show set to launch, but you can’t see the program on its flagship streaming service. The company plans to take over the history Marlborough Pub in London between September 3 and September 5, when it will outfit the place much like its comedic…
whatHappening: Netflix is launching an unconventional marketing campaign for its show 'The Gentlemen' by taking over London's historic Marlborough Pub from September 3-5. Rather than promoting the program on its streaming service, the company is transforming the physical pub space to match the show's aesthetic and world.
whoInvolved: Netflix, the global streaming giant, is partnering with Stella Artois, a Belgian pilsner beer owned by Anheuser-Busch InBev. The campaign centers on 'The Gentlemen,' a comedic show set to launch on the platform.
whyMatters: This partnership represents an evolution in how streaming services market content, moving beyond digital channels into experiential, real-world activations that blend entertainment with consumer brands. The strategy suggests Netflix is willing to invest in immersive marketing to build buzz for major releases, particularly by leveraging iconic venues and established beer brands to reach audiences offline.
articleBody:
Netflix is taking an unconventional approach to promoting its latest show by partnering with beer brand Stella Artois for an experiential marketing takeover at London's historic Marlborough Pub. Between September 3 and September 5, the streaming service will transform the venue to reflect the world of 'The Gentlemen,' its upcoming comedic series. Rather than relying solely on traditional digital promotion through its platform, Netflix is betting that physical, immersive brand experiences will generate word-of-mouth buzz and cultural conversation.

The partnership pairs Netflix with Stella Artois, a pilsner beer first brewed in 1926 by Brouwerij Artois in Leuven, Belgium. The beer has maintained its original 5.2 percent ABV standard and is now distributed globally, including across the UK market where this activation is taking place. Stella Artois is owned by Interbrew International B.V., a subsidiary of Anheuser-Busch InBev, the world's largest brewer. The brand's long heritage and premium positioning align with the pub setting and the comedic tone suggested by the show's title.

This marketing mash-up reflects a broader shift in how streaming services seek to cut through digital noise. According to Variety, Netflix is outfitting the Marlborough Pub to immerse visitors in the aesthetic and tone of 'The Gentlemen.' By choosing a real London pub rather than a temporary pop-up, Netflix leverages the venue's existing cultural cachet and draws in both dedicated fans and curious passersby who might not otherwise encounter the show's promotional material online.

The strategy also signals how entertainment companies increasingly view alcohol brands as natural partners in experiential marketing. The association between a prestigious beer brand and a new television show creates multiple layers of appeal: existing Stella Artois drinkers may become curious about the show, while the pub itself becomes a destination for fans seeking an authentic connection to the content they're about to watch.

With the campaign set to run for just three days in early September, the activation appears designed to generate concentrated media attention and social sharing rather than serve as a long-term promotional venue. The limited timeframe creates urgency and exclusivity, encouraging people to visit during the window or hear about the experience through friends and media coverage.

title: How the Muppets Were Brought Back to Life for the Disney Special
summary: The lights were lit and the music played in the Muppet Theatre once more this year. But before the curtain opened on Kermit the Frog in an episode of television for the first time in 10 years, the show had to be put together — by the humans behind the characters. Simultaneously…
whatHappening: The Muppets have returned to television for the first time in a decade with a new Disney special. Behind the scenes, the puppeteers and production team had to reassemble the iconic characters and rebuild the machinery of the Muppet Theatre to bring the show to life.
whoInvolved: Disney, which acquired the Muppets franchise from the Jim Henson Company in 2004 and established the Muppets Studio to oversee the characters. The production involves the puppeteers and crew who operate the characters that have defined the franchise since Jim Henson created them in 1955.
whyMatters: This revival marks a significant moment for a beloved American entertainment institution that has been largely absent from television. The return signals Disney's continued investment in reviving classic Muppet content and demonstrates the technical and creative challenges involved in maintaining these characters for modern audiences.
articleBody:
The Muppet Theatre's lights flickered back on this year as Disney prepared to reintroduce Kermit the Frog and his ensemble cast to television audiences for the first time in a decade. According to Variety, the production required extensive behind-the-scenes work to resurrect not just the characters themselves, but the entire mechanical and creative infrastructure that brings them to life on screen.

The Muppets, an American ensemble cast known for their absurdist, slapstick, and self-referential comedy style, were created by Jim Henson in 1955 and became a cornerstone of American television and film. The Jim Henson Company maintained creative control of the characters for nearly five decades before Disney acquired the franchise in 2004, establishing the Muppets Studio division to oversee the characters' development and appearances across film, television, music, and other media.

Bringing the Muppets back to television required the coordination of puppeteers, technicians, and production crews who work in tandem to operate the characters and navigate the technical demands of modern production. The challenge extended beyond simply dusting off old puppets; the team had to reassemble the sets, coordinate the intricate mechanics of puppet operation, and ensure the characters remained authentic to their original design and performance style while meeting contemporary production standards.

The ten-year absence from television represents one of the longest gaps in the Muppets' performance history. During that time, the characters appeared in films and occasional specials, but the regular television presence that defined their cultural impact had largely disappeared, leaving a generation of viewers with limited exposure to the characters in their original variety-show format.

This new Disney special represents a test of whether audiences still connect with the Muppets' particular brand of humor and entertainment. It also reflects Disney's broader strategy of reviving legacy franchises and characters for contemporary media platforms, leveraging the company's resources and distribution capabilities to reintroduce beloved properties to both nostalgic longtime fans and new viewers.

articleBody:
Gersh and Other Angle Pictures have boarded Israeli filmmaker Avi Nesher's feature 'Our Loves' for international sales representation. Israel's Oscar submission process typically culminates with a final selection announced later in the year, and positioning 'Our Loves' through established sales agencies early in the cycle strengthens its candidacy. International feature submissions often benefit from pre-existing distribution relationships and festival exposure, both of which can be accelerated through coordinated sales representation.

The film's traction in the sales market underscores the continued appetite for international cinema among distributors and audiences, even as the competitive landscape for Academy consideration remains intense.

whatHappening: The 31st Busan International Film Festival has announced its Korean Cinema Today and On Screen selections, featuring Na Hong-Jin's thriller 'Hope' alongside eight other films across multiple categories. The lineups showcase a mix of high-profile releases and festival premieres from South Korean cinema.
whoInvolved: Na Hong-Jin is a celebrated South Korean director known for violent thrillers and horror elements, with breakthrough successes including The Chaser (2008) and The Yellow Sea (2010). The Busan International Film Festival, held annually in Busan since 1996, is one of Asia's most significant film festivals and the first international film festival established in South Korea.
whyMatters: These selections highlight the current state of Korean cinema at a major Asian festival platform, with Na Hong-Jin's latest work drawing international attention ahead of theatrical release. Festival premieres and industry showcases like these influence global distribution deals, critical reception, and the trajectory of Korean films in international markets.
articleBody:
The 31st Busan International Film Festival has unveiled its Korean Cinema Today and On Screen selections, cementing the event's role as a major showcase for domestic South Korean talent. Na Hong-Jin's 'Hope' headlines a nine-film lineup that spans both the Panorama and Special Premiere sections, drawing significant global attention even before its wider theatrical release. According to Variety, the festival's curation reflects the breadth and ambition of current Korean filmmaking across multiple genres and formats.

Na Hong-Jin has established himself as one of South Korea's most distinctive voices through a filmography defined by violent thrillers and horror elements. His 2008 feature debut, The Chaser, became a watershed moment for the director, achieving both critical acclaim and commercial success as the third-highest-grossing film in South Korea that year. The Yellow Sea followed in 2010, earning international recognition when it was selected for the Un Certain Regard section at the Cannes Film Festival, further solidifying Na's reputation as a filmmaker capable of commanding global stages.

Beyond Na's 'Hope,' the Korean Cinema Today and On Screen selections include Netflix's 'Dead-End Job' and 'Blue Road,' as well as Disney+'s 'The Remarked Empress,' signaling the growing influence of streaming platforms in shaping Korean cinema's international profile. This mix of theatrical releases and platform-exclusive content reflects broader shifts in how Korean films reach audiences globally and how festivals position themselves within an evolving media landscape.

The Busan International Film Festival, held annually in Haeundae District since its inaugural event in September 1996, has long served as a crucial venue for Korean cinema. As the first international film festival established in South Korea, it has consistently championed domestic filmmakers while providing a gateway for Korean works to reach international buyers, critics, and audiences. The festival's emphasis on Korean Cinema Today programming demonstrates its continued commitment to celebrating and elevating current homegrown talent.

The announcement of these selections underscores the festival's influence in shaping the year's conversation around Korean film exports and industry recognition. For filmmakers like Na Hong-Jin, a Busan premiere or special selection can significantly amplify a film's visibility among international distributors and press. The inclusion of major streaming titles alongside traditional theatrical releases also reflects how Korean cinema now operates across multiple exhibition platforms simultaneously.

title: Taylor Swift Recalls How ‘I Knew You Were Trouble’ Was Written As a ‘Really Sad Ballad’ in Grammy Museum Conversation Video
summary: Taylor Swift opened up about the process of writing and recording her 2012 hit “I Knew You Were Trouble,” revealing that it was initially penned as a “really sad ballad” before she was encouraged to incorporate dubstep. Swift reflected on the song’s creation during a Q&A at the…
whatHappening: Taylor Swift is discussing the creative origins of her 2012 hit 'I Knew You Were Trouble,' revealing during a Grammy Museum conversation that the song began as a melancholic ballad before being transformed into a dubstep-influenced pop track.
whoInvolved: Taylor Swift is the American singer-songwriter behind the track, which was co-written and produced by Max Martin and Shellback for her fourth studio album Red. The conversation took place at the Grammy Museum, a cultural institution dedicated to music history and achievement.
whyMatters: Swift's insight into the song's evolution highlights the critical role producers play in shaping a track's final sound and commercial identity. The track became notable for its radical sonic departure from Swift's country-pop roots, making this behind-the-scenes account valuable for understanding how artistic collaboration and production choices can fundamentally alter a song's impact and reception.
articleBody:
Taylor Swift opened up about the surprising creative journey behind "I Knew You Were Trouble," one of her most distinctive hits from the 2012 album Red. During a Q&A conversation at the Grammy Museum, Swift revealed that the song was originally composed as "a really sad ballad" before undergoing a significant sonic transformation.

The track, co-written and produced by Max Martin and Shellback, eventually emerged as a dubstep and pop creation that marked a striking departure from Swift's established country-pop sound. According to Variety, Swift reflected on how she was encouraged to incorporate dubstep elements into what had begun as a traditional sad ballad. The final recording features a production foundation built around electric guitars and synthesizers, with a wobble bass accentuating the refrain and Swift's distorted vocals giving the track its distinctive electronic character.

Red, Swift's fourth studio album, was conceived as a breakup record chronicling the emotional aftermath of a failed relationship. "I Knew You Were Trouble" fit thematically within that framework, though its production choice proved decidedly unconventional. The song's lyrics maintain the introspective, retrospective tone expected of a breakup narrative, but the dubstep elements created an unexpected sonic context for that emotional content.

Critics at the time noted that the dubstep production represented a radical departure from Swift's previous work, though the song ultimately became one of Red's most memorable tracks. Swift's willingness to experiment with the production aligned with the album's broader emotional range—the project's very title suggested the multiple colors and textures of heartbreak, from anger to sadness to reflection.

The Grammy Museum conversation provides rare insight into the collaborative process between artist and producer, illustrating how initial creative instincts can be substantially reshaped through production decisions. Swift's recollection underscores how the final version of a song often emerges through negotiation and experimentation rather than adhering strictly to an original concept. For fans and music professionals alike, understanding these behind-the-scenes choices offers deeper appreciation for how albums are constructed and refined.

title: Rosie O’Donnell Should Host Her Own Show on Late Night TV — and Shatter Comedy’s Greatest Glass Ceiling
summary: Late night is in the doldrums. It’s not just that the remaining hosts are taking much of the summer off. But, post-Stephen Colbert on CBS, ABC’s Jimmy Kimmel and NBC’s Jimmy Fallon both feel closer to the end of their respective tenures than the beginning. The whole genre feels…
whatHappening: Late-night television is in decline, with established hosts nearing the end of their tenures. A Variety opinion piece argues that Rosie O'Donnell should host her own late-night show, potentially breaking new ground in the genre.
whoInvolved: Rosie O'Donnell, an American comedian and television personality who hosted the Emmy-winning syndicated daytime talk show The Rosie O'Donnell Show from 1996 to 2002. Current late-night hosts Jimmy Kimmel (ABC) and Jimmy Fallon (NBC) are also central to the discussion, as is Stephen Colbert, whose tenure at CBS's The Late Show recently concluded.
whyMatters: The proposal highlights potential opportunities to revitalize a struggling late-night format while addressing representation in a traditionally male-dominated space. A new late-night host could reshape audience expectations and bring fresh creative energy to a genre currently perceived as stagnant and aging.
articleBody:
Late-night television faces a crisis of momentum and relevance. According to Variety, the genre is in the doldrums—not merely because hosts are taking extended summer breaks, but because the fundamental viability of the format itself appears uncertain. Both ABC's Jimmy Kimmel and NBC's Jimmy Fallon feel closer to the end of their respective tenures than the beginning, signaling potential upheaval in a programming category that has long anchored network schedules.

Into this vacuum, the argument emerges that Rosie O'Donnell should be positioned to host a late-night program. O'Donnell brings substantial credentials to such a role. After breaking through on the television series Star Search in 1984, she built a powerful media presence, ultimately hosting The Rosie O'Donnell Show, a syndicated daytime talk program that ran from 1996 to 2002 and won multiple Daytime Emmy Awards. During that run, she cultivated the nickname "Queen of Nice," establishing herself as a relatable personality capable of commanding audiences across demographics.

The late-night landscape has undergone significant transitions in recent years. Stephen Colbert, who transitioned from his acclaimed Comedy Central news satire show The Colbert Report to host CBS's The Late Show, recently concluded his tenure, opening questions about who will shape the genre's future. The proposal to bring O'Donnell into late night represents not merely a personnel decision but a potential reimagining of what late-night comedy and talk can be.

O'Donnell's track record in daytime television suggests she possesses the skills necessary to command a late-night audience. Her earlier show demonstrated an ability to balance comedy, emotional authenticity, and conversation in ways that resonated with viewers. The daytime format, while distinct from late night, required similar skills in interviewing, comedic timing, and audience connection.

The timing of this proposal reflects genuine concern about the viability of late-night television as it currently exists. Networks face pressure to attract younger audiences who increasingly consume content outside traditional broadcast schedules. A fresh voice and perspective in the late-night slot could potentially reverse declining viewership and reignite interest in a format that has weathered technological disruption and changing media consumption habits for decades.

title: ‘Emomee,’ Indian Kids Life-Skills Series, Lands on Netflix (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: An Indian children’s entertainment company has brought its debut original animated series to Netflix. “Emomee: Big Skills for Little Ones, Minis,” from the Mumbai-based brand Emomee, features 20 episodes of some 11 minutes each, centered on characters E, Mo and Mee as they…
whatHappening: Indian children's entertainment company Emomee has launched its debut animated series on Netflix. The show, titled "Emomee: Big Skills for Little Ones, Minis," consists of 20 episodes designed to teach life skills to young viewers.
whoInvolved: Emomee is a Mumbai-based children's entertainment brand making its first original animated series. Netflix is an American subscription streaming service that distributes original and acquired content internationally across multiple languages and genres.
whyMatters: The deal represents growth in Netflix's portfolio of children's content from Indian creators and reflects the platform's expansion into localized educational programming. It signals Netflix's continued investment in original content from emerging markets while positioning Emomee to reach a global audience through the streaming platform's international reach.
articleBody:
Emomee, a Mumbai-based children's entertainment company, has secured a deal to bring its debut original animated series to Netflix. According to Variety, the series, titled "Emomee: Big Skills for Little Ones, Minis," comprises 20 episodes of approximately 11 minutes each, following three main characters named E, Mo, and Mee as they navigate various scenarios designed to build life skills in young audiences.

The show marks a significant milestone for Emomee as it makes the transition from concept to global distribution. By partnering with Netflix, an American subscription video-on-demand streaming service available internationally in multiple languages, the company gains access to millions of households across dozens of countries. title: ‘Boorman and the Devil’ Review: The Making of John Boorman’s 1977 Disaster ‘Exorcist II: The Heretic’ Becomes a Documentary So Unbelievable It’s Funny
summary: You might call Boorman’s fortitude admirable, but you could also call it delusional. And it lends "Boorman and the Devil" the quality of a true-life Christopher Guest movie. For this is the unintentionally funny story of what happens when utterly unhinged and high-minded hubris…
whatHappening: A new documentary titled 'Boorman and the Devil' examines the chaotic production of John Boorman's infamous 1977 film 'Exorcist II: The Heretic,' revealing the director's delusional creative ambitions that resulted in unintentional comedy.
whoInvolved: John Boorman is a acclaimed British filmmaker known for classics like 'Deliverance' (1972), 'Zardoz' (1974), and 'Excalibur' (1981). The documentary focuses on his ill-fated sequel to William Goodhart's 1973 horror hit 'The Exorcist,' which starred Linda Blair and Richard Burton.
whyMatters: The documentary reveals how even established auteurs can produce critically panned films when ambition outpaces execution, offering insight into Hollywood's creative risks and failures. For film historians and fans of cinema history, it documents a fascinating case study in directorial hubris and the gap between artistic vision and audience reception.
articleBody:
A new documentary is shedding light on one of cinema's most notorious production disasters: John Boorman's 1977 sequel 'Exorcist II: The Heretic.' The film, which starred Linda Blair, Richard Burton, and Louise Fletcher, became a punchline in horror history, but according to Variety, the story of its making is so absurd it reads like a Christopher Guest mockumentary brought to life.

Boorman, a filmmaker with an impressive track record including 'Deliverance' and the visionary sci-fi oddity 'Zardoz,' approached the sequel with what can only be described as unhinged ambition. Rather than deliver a straightforward follow-up to the 1973 original, Boorman attempted to transform the horror franchise into something entirely different—a high-minded supernatural science fiction film that bore little resemblance to what audiences expected or wanted. His fortitude in pursuing this vision might be admirable in abstract terms, but 'Boorman and the Devil' documents the results as something closer to delusional filmmaking.

The documentary captures the dark comedy of watching a respected director become consumed by his own grandiose vision. Set four years after the events of the original film, 'Exorcist II' attempted to expand the mythology in ways that contemporary audiences found baffling rather than terrifying. The film's notorious reputation has only grown with time, becoming a cultural reference point for ambitious sequels that fundamentally misunderstand their source material.

What makes the documentary compelling is how it traces the gap between intention and execution. Boorman's commitment to his vision remained unwavering even as the production descended into chaos and the finished film faced near-universal dismissal. The documentary presents this not as a tale of noble failure, but as a cautionary study in how utterly unhinged creative hubris can produce something inadvertently hilarious.

For film historians, 'Exorcist II: The Heretic' has long been fertile ground for analysis—a case where a major studio greenlit and released a major star vehicle that audiences and critics rejected almost universally. Boorman would go on to direct 'Excalibur' in 1981, proving his commercial recovery was possible, but the shadow of the 1977 sequel has never entirely lifted from his filmography.

title: Vertical Media on Track to Generate $150 Billion in 2026 as the Booming Sector Fights Crowded Content Field and High Subscriber Acquisition Costs
summary: There’s no doubt that 2026 will go down as a milestone year for the growth in popularity of vertical media content in the U.S. The sector is booming but still incredibly diffuse. That will change as microdramas and other formats proliferate and generate more advertising,…
whatHappening: Vertical media is surging toward a $150 billion market in 2026, establishing itself as a major force in entertainment. The sector is experiencing explosive growth despite challenges from content saturation and rising costs to acquire subscribers.
whoInvolved: The vertical media sector encompasses content creators, streaming platforms, and advertisers investing in short-form video and microdrama formats optimized for mobile viewing. whyMatters: Vertical media's projected $150 billion revenue milestone signals a fundamental shift in how entertainment is produced, distributed, and monetized in the digital age. This growth reshapes advertising strategies and subscriber acquisition models while intensifying competition in an already crowded content landscape, forcing platforms to innovate rapidly or risk obsolescence.
articleBody:
Vertical media is on track to become a $150 billion industry by 2026, marking a watershed moment for a sector that has quietly transformed entertainment consumption in the United States. The growth reflects a seismic shift in how audiences engage with content, particularly as smartphone usage continues to dominate leisure time across demographic groups.

The vertical video format—content designed specifically for vertical phone screens rather than traditional horizontal displays—has moved from a niche novelty to mainstream entertainment infrastructure. Microdramas, short-form comedy, and other vertical-native content categories are proliferating across platforms, each competing for viewer attention and advertising dollars. According to Variety, the sector is booming but remains incredibly diffuse, with fragmentation across numerous platforms and creators limiting consolidation around dominant players.

However, the path to profitability remains treacherous. Platforms face two critical headwinds that could constrain growth: a dangerously crowded content marketplace where differentiation becomes increasingly difficult, and the escalating costs of subscriber acquisition in a saturated market. With thousands of vertical media creators and platforms competing for finite viewer attention, standing out requires constant innovation and significant marketing investment. The economics of content production at scale have become punishing, forcing many players to seek partnerships or consolidation.

Advertising represents the primary revenue lever driving the sector toward that $150 billion projection. Unlike subscription-based models that struggle with churn and customer acquisition costs, advertising-supported vertical content can monetize engagement more directly. As microdramas and other formats mature and gain production sophistication, they become increasingly attractive to brand advertisers seeking younger, mobile-first audiences. This advertising growth is expected to accelerate as measurement and targeting capabilities improve across vertical platforms.

The 2026 milestone will likely coincide with significant consolidation within the sector. Smaller platforms lacking either premium content pipelines or sustainable advertising models will face pressure to merge, while well-funded ventures with proven audience traction will expand their footprints. This shakeout could finally impose order on what currently remains a diffuse, fragmented marketplace of competing visions for how vertical content should be produced and distributed.

For major media companies and tech giants, vertical media represents both opportunity and threat. The $150 billion projection underscores that ignoring this sector is no longer viable, yet competing successfully requires different strategies than traditional entertainment. The next 18 months will determine which platforms emerge as sustainable winners in vertical media's booming but treacherous ecosystem.

title: ‘Good People’ Review: Milcho Manchevski’s Haunting Documentary Revisits the Kočani Nightclub Fire Through Survivors’ Eyes
summary: On March 16, 2025, a fire broke out at the Pulse nightclub in the small North Macedonian town of Kočani, injuring hundreds and killing 63 people due to burn damage, smoke inhalation and other physical traumas sustained while attendees scrambled to flee through the venue’s sole…
whatHappening: Filmmaker Milcho Manchevski has created a documentary called 'Good People' that examines the Kočani nightclub fire through the perspectives of survivors. The film revisits the March 2025 tragedy that killed 63 people in North Macedonia.
whoInvolved: Milcho Manchevski is a Macedonian-American film director, photographer, and artist who has now documented this disaster through survivor testimony. The film centers on those who lived through the Pulse nightclub fire in the small North Macedonian town of Kočani.
whyMatters: The documentary provides a survivor-centered narrative of a preventable tragedy, potentially holding attention to the safety failures and negligence that enabled the disaster. articleBody:
On March 16, 2025, a fire at the Pulse nightclub in Kočani, North Macedonia, became one of the country's deadliest disasters in recent memory, claiming 63 lives and injuring 193 others. Now, filmmaker Milcho Manchevski has turned his lens toward the survivors, creating a documentary titled 'Good People' that examines the tragedy through their eyes and experiences. According to Variety, the film offers a haunting revisitation of that night, prioritizing the voices and perspectives of those who escaped the inferno.

The fire ignited when sparks from indoor fireworks struck the nightclub's ceiling, rapidly enveloping the venue in thick, toxic smoke. Attendees faced a desperate scramble to flee, hampered by the building's catastrophic safety failures. The nightclub was unlicensed and violated numerous safety codes: it lacked sprinklers, had insufficient emergency exits, and contained only a single fire extinguisher. Most critically, the venue had only one exit route available to patrons—a bottleneck that turned the evacuation into a life-or-death struggle as hundreds rushed toward the sole means of escape.

Manchevski, a Macedonian-American artist known for his work as a director and photographer, has focused 'Good People' on survivor testimony rather than official investigations or institutional blame. This approach centers human experience and recovery, allowing those who lived through the disaster to define its meaning and legacy. By platforming survivor narratives, the documentary shifts focus from abstract discussions of negligence to the concrete, ongoing impact of the tragedy on individual lives.

The film arrives at a moment when questions about venue safety, regulatory oversight, and accountability remain unresolved in North Macedonia and across the region. The Pulse nightclub's violations—its lack of proper licensing, absence of fire suppression systems, and inadequate exits—represent systemic failures that extend beyond a single building. Manchevski's documentary may serve as both memorial and indictment, ensuring that the stories of those affected are preserved and heard.

As 'Good People' circulates, it underscores the importance of survivor-led narratives in documenting tragedy. Rather than allowing institutional or bureaucratic accounts to dominate the historical record, Manchevski has chosen to center those whose lives were forever changed by the fire, offering audiences an intimate understanding of resilience and loss in the aftermath of preventable catastrophe.

The deal also underscores the growing maturity of India's digital content production infrastructure. The company's focus on original content development and creator partnerships positions it to tap into the growing roster of digital creators seeking professional-grade production support and distribution opportunities. By structuring deals around creator ownership, Odyssey aims to differentiate itself in a competitive market where many traditional studios maintain tight control over IP.

The implications of this model extend beyond individual creator success. As production companies experiment with new partnership structures, they may influence broader industry practices around creator compensation and rights. The division's success could demonstrate whether creator-friendly IP models are commercially viable at scale, potentially encouraging other production companies to reconsider how they structure deals with emerging talent.

For creators considering partnerships with production companies, Odyssey's new division offers a template that prioritizes their long-term interests. As the creator economy continues to mature, such arrangements may become increasingly common as a way to attract and retain top talent.
